title: Small Business
headline: Part 19, rewritten. What changed for small business.
subhead: The current rule and the rewrite, side by side, in plain English.
description: FAR Part 19 under the FAR overhaul: 17 changes for small business, side by side with the current rule, plus what did not change, which agencies have adopted it, and what to do now.
shortVersion: Set-asides of orders under multiple-award contracts stay discretionary, and a decision not to set one aside can no longer be protested.
The rule of two still governs contracts, but the FAR no longer tells contracting officers to consider 8(a), HUBZone, SDVOSB or WOSB programs first.

Until a final rule takes effect, the rewrite reaches a contract only through an agency's class deviation and the clauses in that contract. The status line above shows where the formal rulemaking stands.

modelTextUpdates.what: Supplemental model deviation (Supplement 1): eSRS replaced by SAM.gov Subcontracting Plan Reporting (SPR); ISR due date 30 to 45 days; manual CO review/reject steps removed.

dod.revisionSummary: Supersedes the Jan 21, 2026 deviation and SDVOSB deviation 2024-O0002 Rev 1; adopts SAM.gov SPR reporting; uses DFARS 219.106-70 for SDVOSB eligibility checks until SAM.gov aligns; corrects DFARS 219.208-2 threshold from $150M to $100M.

changes.topic: Set-asides of orders under multiple-award contracts
changes.before: Order set-asides are discretionary, but the CO must state in the solicitation and contract whether order set-asides will be discretionary or mandatory when the rule of two is met; a mandatory version uses 52.219-13 Alternate I (FAR 19.504(a)(1), 19.507(f)(2)).
changes.after: Order set-asides stay discretionary, and the CO's decision to set aside or not set aside an order is stated to be not a basis for protest; 52.219-13 Alternate I is marked [Reserved] (RFO 19.111-2(a); RFO 52.219-13).
changes.whatItMeans: Where a vehicle carries the rewritten clause (a new award, or an existing contract modified to add it), a small business can't rely on language committing the agency to set aside qualifying orders, and challenging a decision not to set one aside gets much harder. Agency adoption alone doesn't change an awarded contract: check your vehicle's clauses and modifications. The FAR Companion says the wording is meant to settle a GAO vs. Court of Federal Claims split over the rule of two on multiple-award contracts.
changes.whoItHits: Small business holders of multiple-award contracts (MAS, GWACs, IDIQs)

changes.before: Acquisitions above the micro-purchase threshold up to the SAT are automatically set aside for small business unless the CO lacks a reasonable expectation of two competitive small offerors; above the SAT the CO must set aside when that expectation exists (FAR 19.502-2(a)-(b)).
changes.after: For contracts above the micro-purchase threshold, the CO must set the contract aside when there is a reasonable expectation of offers from two or more responsible, competitive small businesses, and must document a decision not to (RFO 19.104-1(a)-(b)). The word 'acquisition' became 'contract', and the Practitioner Album says the rule of two does not apply to orders.
changes.whatItMeans: For standalone contracts the set-aside obligation is essentially the same; the FAR Council kept it above the SAT even though only the MPT-to-SAT band is statutory. The real change is the explicit carve-out of orders (see the order set-aside item).
changes.whoItHits: All small businesses bidding standalone contracts

changes.before: Above the SAT the CO shall first consider 8(a), HUBZone, SDVOSB or WOSB before a small business set-aside (FAR 19.203(c)); the CO shall consider HUBZone, SDVOSB and WOSB sole-source awards before a small business set-aside (FAR 19.1306(a), 19.1406(a), 19.1506(a)); for orders above the SAT the same order applies (FAR 19.504(a)(3)).
changes.after: FAR 19.203 'Relationship among small business programs' is removed; the small business set-aside is mandatory when the rule of two is met, and it 'does not preclude' awards under the HUBZone, SDVOSB, WOSB or 8(a) programs (RFO 19.104-1(e)). Socioeconomic sole sources become 'may consider' (RFO 19.105-3(a), 19.106-3(a), 19.107-3(a)), and the order-level priority is not carried over (RFO 19.111-2).
changes.whatItMeans: Socioeconomic set-asides and sole sources remain available, but the FAR no longer tells COs to look at them before an ordinary small business set-aside. Expect more plain small business set-asides where a HUBZone, SDVOSB, WOSB or 8(a) firm might previously have been considered first.

changes.before: Contractors must rerepresent size and socioeconomic status for the NAICS code of certain orders (e.g., a socioeconomic set-aside order under an unrestricted MAC), and the CO may require rerepresentation for any order; agency goal credit follows the order rerepresentation (FAR 19.301-2(b)(2)-(3), (d)(2)).
changes.after: Rerepresentation is triggered only by contract-level events: novation, merger or acquisition, and the long-term-contract checkpoints (year five and each later option) (RFO 19.301(a); RFO 52.219-28(b)). Agency credit is driven by the contract-level size status (GSA RFO-2025-19 memo; Practitioner Album).
changes.whatItMeans: The FAR's own order-level rerepresentation triggers are gone, so fewer orders will ask you to recertify size through the FAR process. SBA's size rules still decide whether you count as small for a particular order, such as a set-aside order under an unrestricted contract (13 CFR 121.404). Check the order's terms before relying on your contract-level status.
changes.whoItHits: Small and recently graduated firms on IDIQs/MACs

changes.before: Part 19 itself states the limits: no more than 50% of the amount paid to non-similarly-situated subcontractors for services and for supplies (excluding materials), 85% for general construction and 75% for special trades, with compliance periods (FAR 19.505(a)-(b)).
changes.after: The same percentages and compliance periods now sit in the clause itself (RFO 52.219-14(e)-(f)); Part 19 keeps only the prescription (RFO 19.104-3(c)), with the 8(a) version restated at RFO 19.108-8. The 'similarly situated entity' definition lives only in the clause.
changes.whatItMeans: The percentages are the same (50/85/75), and they now live in the clause, so read your contract's 52.219-14 (Deviation) text rather than looking for them in Part 19. For 8(a) awards, the rewritten Part 19 describes the calculation in different terms from the clause, so follow the clause in your contract and ask the contracting officer if the two seem to disagree.
changes.whoItHits: Small primes on set-aside and sole-source work

changes.before: FAR 19.505(c) lists all nonmanufacturer requirements in Part 19: supply a U.S. small-business-made end item, not exceed 500 employees (150 for IT VARs under 541519), be primarily engaged in retail/wholesale, and take ownership or possession; plus kit, waiver and multiple-item rules.
changes.after: RFO 19.104-1(f) keeps the small-business-made end item rule, the kit cap, waivers and the 50% multiple-item test; the 'primarily engaged' and ownership/possession duties move into clause 52.219-33(c); the 500/150-employee cap appears in 52.219-28(d) and SBA's rule (13 CFR 121.406(b)(1)(i)); 'identification of manufacturers' moves to FAR Companion FC 19.104-1(f).
changes.whatItMeans: Resellers face the same substantive test, but it is now spread across Part 19, two clauses, SBA's regulation and the Companion. Check all of them before relying on a nonmanufacturer strategy.

changes.before: For contracts other than MACs, the CO 'shall set aside a portion or portions' when a total set-aside isn't appropriate and the listed conditions are met (FAR 19.502-3(a)); partial set-asides of MACs are discretionary (FAR 19.502-4(a)).
changes.after: One unified rule says COs 'may, at their discretion' partially set aside any acquisition except construction when the conditions are met (RFO 19.104-2(a)).
changes.whatItMeans: A big single-award requirement that small firms can only perform in part no longer has to be split to give small businesses a reserved slice. The FAR Council's summary calls the principles identical, but the text moved from 'shall' to 'may'.
changes.whoItHits: Small firms targeting large single-award requirements

changes.topic: 8(a): compete first below the threshold; sole source above it
changes.before: Below the $5.5M ($8.5M manufacturing) competitive threshold, competitive 8(a) awards need approval from SBA's Associate Administrator for Business Development; above it, SBA may accept a sole source if two 8(a) offers aren't expected or the firm is tribally/ANC-owned (FAR 19.805-1(b), (d)).
changes.after: Below the threshold, COs must first try a competitive 8(a) order on SBA-approved government-wide contracts before going sole source (RFO 19.108-7(d)(1)); above it, SBA may accept a sole source only after the CO meets the Part 6 other-than-full-and-open rules (RFO 19.108-7(b); RFO 6.103).
changes.whatItMeans: Directed 8(a) sole-source awards under the threshold become harder to get where a GWAC with an 8(a) pool exists. 8(a) firms that are not on those vehicles lose ground.
changes.whoItHits: 8(a) participants, especially those relying on sole-source marketing

changes.before: An 8(a) follow-on stays in the program unless SBA's AA/BD agrees in writing to release it (or a mandatory source applies); release is generally granted when the agency will use a SB, HUBZone, SDVOSB or WOSB set-aside (FAR 19.815(a)-(c)).
changes.after: A follow-on is released automatically, with no formal request, if it will be set aside under the HUBZone, SDVOSB or WOSB programs; other releases still need a written request and AA/BD concurrence (RFO 19.108-11(a)-(b)).
changes.whatItMeans: An incumbent 8(a) firm's work can move to a HUBZone, SDVOSB or WOSB competition without SBA weighing its business-development impact. SBA's own regulation still describes a request-and-concurrence process (see conflicts).

changes.before: An offeror with a pending WOSB/EDWOSB certification application may compete on a WOSB/EDWOSB set-aside; if it is the apparent winner, the CO asks SBA for a determination, which SBA makes within 15 calendar days (FAR 19.1505(d)-(f)).
changes.after: For a WOSB/EDWOSB set-aside or sole source, the CO must verify before award that the offeror is designated as certified in SAM; there is no pending-application path in the text (RFO 19.107-1(b); RFO 52.219-29(c), 52.219-30(c)).
changes.whatItMeans: In agencies using the deviation, women-owned firms should hold an actual certification before bidding on WOSB/EDWOSB set-asides. SBA's rule still allows pending applicants (see conflicts), so expect disputes.
changes.whoItHits: Women-owned firms awaiting SBA or third-party certification

changes.before: An SDVOSB qualifies if it is SBA-certified in SAM or self-represented in SAM and applied to SBA on or before December 31, 2023 (FAR 19.1403(b), 19.1405(c), 19.1406(b)).
changes.after: The CO verifies that the offeror is designated in SAM as an SBA-certified SDVOSB; the 2023 grandfather path is gone (RFO 19.106-1(b); RFO 52.219-27(c)). DoD's Revision 1 deviation uses alternate verification procedures at DFARS 219.106-70 until SAM.gov aligns with the FAR.
changes.whatItMeans: Only SBA-certified SDVOSBs (VetCert) count. Few firms should still be pending from 2023, but any that are are now out.

changes.before: To count under a subcontracting plan, a subcontractor may represent itself as small, VOSB, SDVOSB, HUBZone, SDB or WOSB, and the prime may accept the representation (FAR 19.703(a)).
changes.after: A subcontractor represents itself only as small or SDB; for VOSB, SDVOSB, HUBZone or WOSB it must be certified by SBA (RFO 19.302-2(a)(1)).
changes.whatItMeans: Large primes may stop counting self-certified veteran-owned or woman-owned subs toward socioeconomic goals and favor certified firms. SBA's current rule only bars self-certification for HUBZone and SDVOSB subcontractors, so the scope is contested.
changes.whoItHits: Small subcontractors to large primes (VOSB, WOSB especially)

changes.topic: Subcontracting reports: eSRS to SAM.gov SPR, 45 days
changes.before: ISRs and SSRs go into eSRS; reports are due 30 days after each period ends, and COs must acknowledge or reject them within 60 days (FAR 19.704(a)(10)(iv), 19.705-6(f), (j)).
changes.after: Reports go into Subcontracting Plan Reporting (SPR) at SAM.gov within 45 days after the period ends (e.g., by Nov 14 for the FY ending Sept 30); CO acknowledge/reject steps are removed and agencies set their own monitoring (RFO 19.302-2(a), 19.302-3(f), 19.206-1(c)(4)); this came from the February 20, 2026 supplement.
changes.whatItMeans: Reports move to a new system, SPR at SAM.gov. The 45-day deadline comes from the rewritten clause; the codified FAR still says 30 days. Use 45 days only where your contract carries the deviation clause or the contracting officer says so; otherwise keep to 30.
changes.whoItHits: Other-than-small primes with subcontracting plans; small firms that grew out of size

changes.topic: Small business specialist / PCR review role
changes.before: The contracting activity must coordinate with the agency small business specialist no later than 30 days before issuing a solicitation (FAR 19.201(d)(1)); FAR 19.201(c) lists OSDBU duties; PCRs may review any proposed acquisition above the MPT on request (FAR 19.501(d)) and may pick acquisitions for review at their discretion (FAR 19.202-1(e)(1)(iv)).
changes.after: RFO 19.102 keeps the 30-day package to the PCR for bundled, consolidated or too-large requirements, the 15-day PCR recommendation, the rejection/appeal chain and the OSDBU recommendation review (RFO 19.102(e)-(g)). The specialist 30-day coordination, the OSDBU duty list, the any-acquisition review and the discretionary-review trigger are not in RFO Part 19; the specialist appears only in subcontracting-plan review (RFO 19.206-3(d)(7)) and bundling plans (RFO 7).
changes.whatItMeans: There are fewer built-in checkpoints where an advocate must see a requirement before release. Small firms should take capability briefings to the OSDBU and PCR early instead of counting on a mandatory review.
changes.whoItHits: All small businesses relying on SB advocates in market research

changes.topic: Reserves: direct orders to a sole reserve awardee
changes.before: Under a MAC reserve, if there is only one award to a given type of small business, the CO may issue orders directly to it (FAR 19.504(c)(1)(ii)); clause 52.219-32 implements this (FAR 19.507(g)(2)).
changes.after: Reserves remain discretionary (RFO 19.112), but clause 52.219-32 is removed and there is no direct-order authority; orders under reserves follow the general order set-aside rule (RFO 19.111-2; RFO 52.219-32 [Reserved]).
changes.whatItMeans: Holding the only reserve slot no longer guarantees a path to orders. Reserve awardees must compete for set-aside or unrestricted orders.
changes.whoItHits: Small businesses holding reserve awards on full-and-open MACs

changes.topic: Certificate of Competency: agency appeal path
changes.before: For COCs between $100,000 and $25 million, an agency can appeal SBA's intent to issue a COC to SBA headquarters through its OSDBU; above $25 million SBA HQ offers the agency a review (FAR 19.602-3).
changes.after: FAR 19.602-3 is removed; RFO 19.204 keeps mandatory referral, the 15-business-day hold, and says SBA COCs are final on all elements of responsibility (RFO 19.204(f), (i)).
changes.whatItMeans: In the FAR text, an SBA COC is no longer second-guessed through an agency appeal. Whether SBA's own COC regulation keeps an agency appeal was not checked (see gaps).

changes.before: The 10% factor shall be applied by line item or group of items, other factors are added first, and a tie between a HUBZone firm and a large business goes to the HUBZone firm (FAR 19.1307(c)-(d)).
changes.after: The 10% preference itself stays mandatory in full and open competition (RFO 19.110, 19.207); the line-item method and tie-break move to the FAR Companion as 'should' guidance (FC 19.110).
changes.whatItMeans: HUBZone firms keep the preference, but the tie-break and line-item mechanics are no longer binding regulation. Ask the CO how the factor will be applied.

unchanged.topic: Size standards, NAICS assignment and the October 1, 2028 multi-NAICS MAC date
unchanged.detail: Same rules: one NAICS code per solicitation; for MAC solicitations issued after October 1, 2028, either one NAICS or one per distinct portion/category; size is set as of the initial offer with price; NAICS appeals are due within 10 calendar days.

HUBZone and WOSB/EDWOSB sole sources: $5.5M ($8.5M manufacturing); SDVOSB: $5M ($8.5M manufacturing); 8(a) competitive threshold $5.5M ($8.5M manufacturing); 8(a) sole sources over $30M still need a justification.

unchanged.topic: Subcontracting plan threshold, good-faith test and liquidated damages
unchanged.detail: Plans are still required above $900,000 ($2 million construction) when subcontracting possibilities exist; plans are not required from small businesses; missing goals alone is not bad faith; liquidated damages equal the shortfall.
Interested parties still have 5 business days after notice of the apparent awardee; SBA Area Offices decide within 15 business days; award is held unless the CO determines otherwise in writing.
50% services, 50% supplies (excluding materials), 85% general construction, 75% special trades; similarly situated subs still count as self-performance.

actions.action: List your multiple-award contracts (MAS, GWACs, agency IDIQs) and check each one's order set-aside clause: the mandatory version, or modified to the rewritten clause? Where the rewritten clause applies, plan your pipeline assuming order set-asides are discretionary and not protestable.
If you are a WOSB/EDWOSB with a pending application, finish SBA or third-party certification and confirm it shows in SAM before bidding WOSB set-asides at deviation agencies.
If you subcontract to large primes as a veteran-owned or woman-owned firm, get SBA certification (VetCert or WOSB) so the prime can count you toward its socioeconomic goals.

If you hold a socioeconomic certification, brief OSDBU and SBA PCRs during market research and ask for a HUBZone, SDVOSB, WOSB or 8(a) set-aside in writing, because the FAR no longer tells COs to consider those programs first.
8(a) firms: get on SBA-approved government-wide vehicles that allow 8(a) order competition, since below-threshold work must be tried there before a sole source.

If you hold a subcontracting plan, first check whether your contract carries the deviation 52.219-9 or the codified clause (or ask the CO). File in SPR at SAM.gov, and calendar 45 days only where the deviation clause or the CO says so; otherwise 30.

agencyDates.agency: Department of Housing and Urban Development

faq.q: Are order set-asides still required under the new FAR Part 19?
faq.a: Not where the rewrite applies. Under the model text, setting aside an order on a multiple-award contract is up to the contracting officer, and that choice is not a basis for protest. An awarded contract keeps the clauses it has until it is modified, so check yours. The rule of two still applies to standalone contracts.

faq.q: Does the rule of two still apply to small business contracts?
faq.a: Yes. For contracts above the micro-purchase threshold, the CO must set the contract aside when two or more responsible small businesses are expected to make competitive offers, and must document a decision not to. The FAR Council kept this above the SAT even though only the band below the SAT is statutory.

faq.q: Do I still have to rerepresent my size for task orders?
faq.a: The FAR's order-level triggers are gone in the model text: rerepresentation follows contract-level events (a novation, a merger or acquisition, and the long-term-contract checkpoints at year five and each later option). SBA's size rules still apply to some orders, such as set-aside orders under unrestricted contracts, so read each order's terms.

faq.q: Did the limitations on subcontracting change in the FAR overhaul?
faq.a: The percentages did not: 50% for services and supplies, 85% for general construction and 75% for special trades. They moved out of Part 19 and into the 52.219-14 clause, so read the clause in your contract. For 8(a) awards, the rewritten Part 19 words the calculation differently from the clause; follow the clause and ask the contracting officer if they seem to conflict.

faq.q: Can a women-owned business with a pending WOSB certification still bid on WOSB set-asides?
faq.a: The current codified FAR and SBA's rule allow it, but the RFO model text requires the CO to verify the firm is certified in SAM before award, with no pending-application path. If you are pursuing WOSB or EDWOSB set-asides at an agency using the deviation, get certified first.

faq.q: Is the new FAR Part 19 actually in effect?
faq.a: It is in effect agency by agency through class deviations. For example, GSA's took effect November 3, 2025 and DoD's February 1, 2026. It is not yet codified: as of November 2, 2026, no proposed rule for Part 19 appears in the Federal Register.

faq.q: What happened to eSRS subcontracting reports?
faq.a: Under the February 20, 2026 update to the model text, reports go to Subcontracting Plan Reporting (SPR) in SAM.gov, and the rewritten clause gives primes 45 days after each period instead of 30. The codified FAR still says eSRS and 30 days, so check which clause your contract carries.
